blocks.text: “THE BELOVED PHYSICIAN” (COLOSSIANS 4:14)
Luke. Named three times, by Paul; by early tradition the writer of the Gospel and Acts.
ALSO CALLED
Lucas
FROM
Scripture does not say
TRADE
A physician: “Luke, the beloved physician”.
FAMILY
Paul lists Aristarchus, Marcus and Jesus called Justus as those “of the circumcision”, then names Epaphras, Luke and Demas separately.
WRITINGS
The Gospel according to Luke (its traditional title) · The Acts of the Apostles (by the same tradition)
BACKGROUND
Home, trade and family
TRADE
FAMILY
From the textPaul lists Aristarchus, Marcus and Jesus called Justus as those “of the circumcision”, then names Epaphras, Luke and Demas separately. Colossians 4:10–14
Scholars' viewFrom that list Smith (1884), Schaff (1890) and Robertson (ISBE, 1915) conclude that Luke was a Gentile. Colossians 4:11 Colossians 4:14 [20][18][25]
WHERE HE WENT
Acts and after
Dashed pins are places known only from later tradition, not from Scripture.
Rome · With Paul in his last imprisonment (2 Timothy). 2 Timothy 1:17 2 Timothy 4:11
Antioch in Syria · tradition · His family's city or birthplace in Eusebius (about 325) and Jerome (about 392) (tradition).
Troas · tradition · Where “we” begins. Luke is placed here only if he is the “we” of Acts (as Irenaeus, about 180, says he was). Acts 16:8–11 Acts 20:6

Philippi · tradition · Where “we” stops and starts again; Robertson (ISBE) takes it as his home. Luke is placed here only if he is the “we” of Acts (as Irenaeus, about 180, says he was). Acts 16:12–17 Acts 20:6
Miletus · tradition · Luke is placed here only if he is the “we” of Acts (as Irenaeus, about 180, says he was). Acts 20:15
Tyre · tradition · Luke is placed here only if he is the “we” of Acts (as Irenaeus, about 180, says he was). Acts 21:3–6
Caesarea · tradition · Luke is placed here only if he is the “we” of Acts (as Irenaeus, about 180, says he was). Acts 21:8
Jerusalem · tradition · Luke is placed here only if he is the “we” of Acts (as Irenaeus, about 180, says he was). Acts 21:17–18
Malta (Melita) · tradition · Luke is placed here only if he is the “we” of Acts (as Irenaeus, about 180, says he was). Acts 28:1
Puteoli · tradition · Luke is placed here only if he is the “we” of Acts (as Irenaeus, about 180, says he was). Acts 28:13–14
Constantinople · tradition · no map pin · Where his bones were laid, says Jerome, about 392 (tradition).
IN ACTS AND THE LETTERS
Paul sends greetings from “Luke, the beloved physician, and Demas”. Colossians 4:14
To Philemon Paul names “Marcus, Aristarchus, Demas, Lucas, my fellowlabourers”. Philemon 1:24
In 2 Timothy, a prisoner in Rome, Paul writes that Demas has forsaken him, Crescens and Titus have gone, and “Only Luke is with me”. 2 Timothy 1:17 2 Timothy 4:10–11

From the textThe narrative of Acts turns to “we” at Troas (Acts 16:10) and leaves it after Philippi (16:17); “we” returns at 20:5 and runs to Jerusalem (21:18), and again from 27:1 to Rome (28:16). The narrator is not named. Acts 16:10–17 Acts 20:5–21:18 Acts 27:1–28:16

From the textIn those passages the narrator sails from Troas to Philippi and speaks to the women by the river there; sails from Philippi to Troas, Miletus, Tyre and Caesarea; goes up to Jerusalem and in “unto James”; and takes the voyage with Paul, the shipwreck at Melita and the road to Rome. Acts 16:11–13 Acts 20:5–6 Acts 20:15 Acts 21:3 Acts 21:8 Acts 21:17–18 +3 more
COMPANIONS
Who was with him
Each line joins him to someone Scripture places beside him.
Paul Calls him “the beloved physician” and a fellowlabourer; “Only Luke is with me”. Colossians 4:14 Philemon 1:24 2 Timothy 4:11
Demas Named beside him twice; later “hath forsaken me”. Colossians 4:14 Philemon 1:24 2 Timothy 4:10
Mark Sends greetings with him; Paul asks Timothy to bring Mark when “Only Luke is with me”. Colossians 4:10 Philemon 1:24 2 Timothy 4:11
Aristarchus A fellowlabourer named with him. Colossians 4:10 Philemon 1:24
Epaphras Named beside him among Paul's greeters. Colossians 4:12 Philemon 1:23
Theophilus From the textThe Gospel and Acts are addressed to him; he is Luke's companion only if Luke wrote them. Luke 1:3 Acts 1:1
HOW THE STORY ENDS
Scripture says, tradition says
SCRIPTURE SAYS
The last we read of him: “Only Luke is with me” (2 Timothy 4:11). Scripture does not record his later life or his death. 2 Timothy 4:11
TRADITION SAYS

Eusebius writes that Luke was “of Antiochian parentage and a physician by profession”, “especially intimate with Paul”, and that he wrote the Gospel and Acts.[1] Who says so: Eusebius, Church History 3.4.7, about AD 325

Jerome calls him “a physician of Antioch” and “companion of all his journeying”, and says he “was buried at Constantinople to which city, in the twentieth year of Constantius, his bones together with the remains of Andrew the apostle were transferred”.[8] Who says so: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 7, about AD 392

A list of “the Seventy” ascribed to Hippolytus makes Luke one of the Seventy, won back by Paul, and says he was “crucified on an olive tree”.[6] Who says so: On the Seventy Apostles, ascribed to Hippolytus, date unknown; its editor calls it “Probably spurious, but yet antique”

Gregory of Nazianzus calls him a martyr and has him work in Achaia; Epiphanius makes him one of the Seventy and has him work in Dalmatia, Gaul, Italy and Macedonia (both as reported by McGiffert, who gives the second “about as much worth as most such traditions”).[2] Who says so: Gregory of Nazianzus and Epiphanius, as reported by McGiffert, 4th century (their dates not checked in a source here)

That Luke was a painter rests, McGiffert writes, on “late tradition, of which the earlier Fathers know nothing”, found in Nicephorus and later writers.[2] Who says so: Nicephorus Callistus, Church History 2.43 (as reported by McGiffert), Byzantine (date not checked here)
WRITINGS
Writings tied to him

READ

OPEN QUESTIONS
Where readers have differed
Luke, Paul's companion, wrote the “we” passages and the whole of Acts
Irenaeus (about 180); the Muratorian fragment; Ramsay (1895); Schaff (1890); Harnack (1907), as reported in the ISBE (1915)

Ramsay: “It is almost universally recognised that the use of the first person … is intentional”. Harnack (Luke the Physician, 1907, as reported in the ISBE) set out the case that the “we” passages share the vocabulary and style of the rest of Luke and Acts. Acts 16:10 Acts 1:1 [16][18][26]
The “we” passages are the work of Timothy
Schleiermacher (1845); Sorof (1890), who gives one source to Luke and one to Timothy; both as reported in the ISBE (1915)
On this view the first-person travel account came from Timothy, who was with Paul on those journeys. Acts 16:1–3 Acts 20:4–5 [26]
A companion's travel account, taken over by a later compiler who was not Paul's companion
“the opposite school” described by McGiffert (1890), who points to Weizsäcker; Holtzmann, who gives Luke the “we” sections only; Schmiedel; both as reported in the ISBE (1915)

McGiffert describes this school as “considering the ‘we’ sections authentic historical accounts from the pen of a companion of Paul, which were afterward incorporated into a larger work by one who was not a pupil of Paul”.[2][26]
IN SCRIPTURE
Every passage
CHAPTERS · 10
Luke 1 Acts 1 Acts 16 Acts 20 Acts 21 Acts 27 Acts 28 Colossians 4 Philemon 1 2 Timothy 4
PASSAGES · 8
Luke 1:1–4 Acts 1:1–2 Acts 16:10–17 Acts 20:5–21:18 Acts 27:1–28:16 Colossians 4:10–14 Philemon 1:23–24 2 Timothy 4:9–11
WHAT SCRIPTURE DOES NOT SAY
Scripture never names the writer of the Gospel of Luke or of Acts.
Scripture does not say where Luke was born or how he came to believe.
Scripture does not say that Luke met Jesus; the Gospel's opening says its writer relied on eyewitnesses (Luke 1:2).
Scripture does not record Luke's death.
IDENTIFICATIONS THIS PAGE RELIES ON

From the textScripture names Luke three times, all in Paul's letters: Colossians 4:14, Philemon 24 (“Lucas”) and 2 Timothy 4:11. The Gospel and Acts never name their writer; both are addressed to Theophilus, and Acts begins by recalling “the former treatise”. Colossians 4:14 Philemon 1:24 2 Timothy 4:11 Luke 1:3 Acts 1:1

Early church · Irenaeus (Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1), 1885Irenaeus is one of the first two witnesses, with the Muratorian fragment, to name this Luke as the writer (McGiffert, 1890): “Luke also, the companion of Paul, recorded in a book the Gospel preached by him”, and he argues from the “we” passages that Luke “was inseparable from Paul”. Acts 16:10 [3][2]

Early church · Unknown (Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 5), 1886The Muratorian fragment says “the well-known physician Luke” wrote the third Gospel “when Paul had associated him with himself”, and that “the Acts of all the Apostles are comprised by Luke in one book”.[5]
Early church · Tertullian (trans. Peter Holmes, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 3), 1885Tertullian calls Luke “not an apostle, but only an apostolic man”, a disciple of Paul.[4]
Scholars' viewSmith (1884) and Robertson (ISBE, 1915) hold that Luke is not the Lucius of Acts 13:1 or Romans 16:21. Acts 13:1 Romans 16:21 [20][25]

Scholars' viewSchaff (1890) rejects the later stories that Luke was one of the Seventy or the companion of Cleopas on the road to Emmaus, because the Gospel's opening shows he was not an eyewitness; McGiffert (1890) rejects the Seventy on the same ground and calls the Emmaus idea an “ingenious but unfounded guess”. Luke 1:2 [2][18]
